clinicalPearls: Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome is a form of post-infectious constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis producing a hyperlucent, hypoperfused lung or lobe that is usually smaller than normal.
It follows a severe lower respiratory infection in early childhood — often viral (adenovirus, measles) or Mycoplasma — that injures the developing distal airways and alveoli.
The classic chest radiograph shows unilateral hyperlucency with a small or normal-sized lung and reduced vascular markings, distinguishing it from compensatory overinflation.
Air trapping is the functional hallmark: expiratory imaging shows the affected side remaining lucent and failing to empty, sometimes with mediastinal shift on expiration.
CT typically reveals mosaic attenuation, bronchiectasis, reduced vessel calibre and areas of low attenuation reflecting the obliterated small airways.
Many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally; others have recurrent infection, chronic cough, exertional dyspnoea or bronchiectasis.
Perfusion imaging demonstrates markedly reduced perfusion to the affected lung, matching the ventilation abnormality.

It must be distinguished from other causes of a unilateral hyperlucent lung, including endobronchial obstruction, congenital lobar emphysema, absent pulmonary artery and prior pneumonectomy or lobar disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome arises when a severe lower respiratory infection during the period of ongoing lung growth in early childhood injures the terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Healing produces constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis, with fibrous narrowing and obliteration of small airways that impairs both ventilation and normal alveolar multiplication in the affected region. The damaged lung is chronically underventilated, and reflex and structural reduction of the pulmonary vascular bed leads to diminished perfusion and attenuated vessels, accounting for the radiographic hyperlucency. Collateral air drift allows air to enter distal units but the obliterated broncholes impede its egress, so air trapping develops and the affected lung fails to deflate normally on expiration. Because the insult occurs during development, the affected lung or lobe often remains smaller than normal, and coexisting bronchiectasis reflects proximal airway damage from the original infection and subsequent recurrent infection.
additionalDifferentials: endobronchial obstruction by tumour or foreign body causing air trapping
congenital absence or hypoplasia of a pulmonary artery
compensatory overinflation after contralateral lobar collapse or resection
bullous or panlobular emphysema (including alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency)
technical or rotational causes of asymmetric radiographic lucency
additionalInvestigations: inspiratory and expiratory CT to demonstrate air trapping and mosaic attenuation
ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy showing matched reduction on the affected side
chest radiograph in inspiration and expiration
pulmonary function testing including assessment of airflow obstruction and gas trapping
bronchoscopy where endobronchial obstruction needs exclusion
CT pulmonary angiography if absent or hypoplastic pulmonary artery is considered
assessment for bronchiectasis-related infection with sputum culture
redFlags: recurrent or severe lower respiratory infections with declining lung function
haemoptysis prompting exclusion of another cause of hyperlucency
progressive dyspnoea suggesting extension of disease or a superimposed process
new focal obstruction raising concern for an endobronchial lesion
reference.prognosis: Many patients remain stable and minimally symptomatic for life, but those with extensive bronchiectasis or recurrent infection may have progressive symptoms; management is largely supportive, with treatment of infection and, rarely, resection for a destroyed lobe causing intractable problems.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the hyperlucency as emphysema, compensatory overinflation or a technical artefact.
Omitting expiratory imaging, without which the diagnostic air trapping may be missed.
Overlooking an endobronchial obstruction that can mimic the appearance.
Failing to recognise and treat associated bronchiectasis and recurrent infection.
Assuming the small hyperlucent lung is congenitally absent tissue rather than post-infectious small-airway obliteration.
references: Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders, current edition
Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine, current edition
Standard thoracic radiology reference texts on the unilateral hyperlucent lung
management: Management is largely supportive, as the obliterative bronchiolitis cannot be reversed
Treat respiratory infections promptly with antimicrobials and ensure influenza and pneumococcal immunisation to prevent further airway damage
Provide airway clearance physiotherapy and manage any associated bronchiectasis
Use inhaled bronchodilators where there is demonstrable airflow obstruction, and advise avoidance of smoking
Monitor with serial pulmonary function testing and review for recurrent infection or progressive symptoms
Reserve surgical resection such as lobectomy for a destroyed lobe causing intractable infection or haemoptysis
